claim: Four streaming subscriptions — Netflix, Disney Plus, Crunchyroll and YouTube Premium — all grade D as convenience purchases in Alan's software audit, and nothing has weighed one against another. No page says what each costs, what each delivers that the others do not, or whether one or two are redundant against the rest. The cluster is among the easiest things in the audit to cancel, and it is worked as one lump with one grade.

evidence:
Read across `alan/book/pages/all-about-alan/topic/pages/` and `.../question/pages/`.

`the-software-i-pay-for-every-month`: "Netflix, Disney Plus, Crunchyroll and YouTube Premium are all D, all convenience, none urgent." That is the whole of it — four names, one grade, one sentence. No page gives a price for any of them, and no page compares what they carry.

`what-leaving-a-dependency-costs-me` places the exit cost: "Medium is days. A streaming service, a recurring subscription." So the book already knows these are cheap to leave.

No question is open on them.

Not measured: "probably redundant" is a hedge I inherited and have not tested — no overlap analysis exists in what I read, and I ran none. That they are among the easiest things to cancel is my reading of the exit-cost band rather than a sentence Alan has written.
